tracks.title: Describing data
tracks.summary: This path is for describing a set of numbers, from averages of center, spread, and shape to pictures of that shape. By the end you can say where they sit, how wide and skewed they are, and whether they look unusual.

steps.title: Mean, Median, and Mode
steps.note: We often describe data by their averages: numerical summaries that answer where the numbers sit. The mean, the median, and the mode are three such answers; they line up when the numbers are roughly balanced, and they pull apart when the shape is not. In the demonstration, move the points and watch which average shifts. When they disagree, the next question is what other kinds of average can capture spread and shape, not only center.
steps.imageAlt: Dot plot of a mildly right-skewed sample. A dotted line marks the mode at 5, a dashed line marks the median at 6, and a solid line marks the mean at 6.94, pulled right by the tail.

steps.title: Moments
steps.note: There are different types of averages, and in statistics those averages of powers of the values (or of their deviations) are called moments. The mean is the first moment; higher moments give numbers for spread and for skew. Compare how each moment responds when you change the sample. Those numbers still treat the sample mean as if it were already known, which matters once variance is estimated from the same data.
steps.imageAlt: Three panels of one sample, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9. The first marks the mean at 4. The second shows squared deviations from that mean, which average to 6.67. The third shows cubed deviations, where the value 9 produces a cube of 125 and the average is 15.

steps.title: Bessel's Correction
steps.note: When we use the data to estimate how spread out they are, the usual average of squared deviations is a little too small, because the sample mean was taken from those same values. Dividing by n − 1 instead of n corrects for that. Run many samples and see which divisor lands nearer the true variance on average. With a fairer number for spread, you can ask whether the shape is pulled one way rather than balanced — that imbalance is skew.
steps.imageAlt: Two bars for the average variance estimate from 8000 samples of size 10, drawn from a population whose variance is 100. Dividing by n averages about 90.2, below the true-variance line. Dividing by n − 1 averages about 100.2, on that line.

steps.title: Skewed Distribution
steps.note: Not every set of numbers is balanced around its center; a long tail on one side pulls the mean toward itself, so mean, median, and mode sit in different places. That imbalance is skew. Drag the skew and watch the three averages separate. A number for skew is useful, but the same shape is easier to see in a picture of how the values pile up and where the middle of the data sits.
steps.imageAlt: A right-skewed density curve. A dotted line marks the mode at 0.49, a dashed line marks the median at 1.00, and a solid line marks the mean at 1.44, farther into the long tail.

steps.title: Boxplot and Histogram
steps.note: Numbers for center, spread, and skew summarize a shape; pictures show that shape directly. A histogram shows how values pile up; a boxplot packs the center and spread of the same data into a box and whiskers. Read the pile and the box together on one sample. Reading both together also shows how far a point can sit before it looks unusual against the middle of the data.
steps.imageAlt: Histogram and boxplot of the same 44 values. The tallest bar is at 5. Dashed lines mark the first quartile at 5, the median at 6, and the third quartile at 8. Whiskers run from 3 to 12.

steps.title: Boxplot and Outliers
steps.note: Once you can see the middle of the data in a boxplot, the next question is which points sit so far out that they count as unusual. The whiskers mark how far a point can sit from the quartiles before it counts as an outlier; the fence is a multiple of the spread inside the box. Add extreme points and watch which ones fall outside the fences. Outliers are one kind of mismatch with a simple shape; another is whether the whole set of numbers matches a reference distribution.
steps.imageAlt: Vertical boxplot for one sample. The box runs from the first quartile at 20 to the third quartile at 40, with the median at 30. Dashed Tukey fences sit at −10 and 70. The upper whisker stops at 44, inside the fence, and a point at 80 is marked as an outlier.

steps.title: Q–Q Plot
steps.note: A few extreme points are one way a set of numbers can look unusual; another is that the overall shape does not match a familiar reference curve. A Q–Q plot lines the sample’s quantiles up against a reference distribution, often the normal. Compare the sample quantiles to the reference line. A curve away from the straight line means the sample’s shape and the reference shape differ — a last check on whether the description you built fits a familiar model.
formulae: plot (theoretical quantile, sample quantile) for each order statistic
steps.imageAlt: Q–Q plot of one sample of 40 standard normal draws. Ordered sample quantiles are plotted against normal theoretical quantiles and lie close to a straight reference line.

tracks.title: Statistical reasoning
tracks.summary: This path is for how a curve for observations becomes a claim about a sample, once sample summaries settle. By the end you can read a confidence interval as long-run coverage, not a chance for one interval.

steps.title: Building the Normal Distribution
steps.note: Many descriptions of data end by asking whether the shape looks like a familiar smooth curve. The normal distribution is one such curve, fixed by a center and a spread. Putting the curve together shows what the model is made of, and sets up the question of what happens to summaries — such as the mean — when you draw many samples.
steps.imageAlt: Standard normal density. A dashed line marks the center at μ = 0. Dotted lines mark one standard deviation on either side, at −1 and 1.

steps.title: Central Limit Theorem (CLT)
steps.note: A single sample mean is one summary of one set of numbers. If you imagine drawing many samples of the same size, those means themselves form a distribution. As each sample gets larger, that distribution of means settles toward a normal curve, whatever shape the raw observations had. The central limit theorem is that statement about means — and classroom simulations make the settling visible.
formulae: X̄ ≈ N(μ, σ²/n) for large n
steps.imageAlt: Sampling distributions of the mean for an exponential population with mean 1. The n = 2 curve is low and right-skewed, n = 8 is taller, and n = 32 is a tall narrow curve on the dashed line at μ = 1.

steps.title: Horowitz (1974) CLT Simulation
steps.note: The central limit theorem is easier to trust when you can watch sample means accumulate. Horowitz's 1974 simulation draws samples again and again in a classroom setting; the collection of sample means takes on a normal shape. Once means behave like normals, sums of squared standard normals become the next building block.
formulae: X̄ₙ → N(μ, σ²/n) as n grows
steps.imageAlt: Histogram of 96 sample means. Each mean is from 10 draws of a normal population with mean 50 and standard deviation 15.8. A normal curve centered at 50 with standard deviation 5 lies over the bars.

steps.title: Chi-Square Distribution
steps.note: Not every sampling story is about a mean. Square independent standard normal draws and add them up; the sum follows a chi-square distribution, the usual sampling model for a variance. With sampling distributions for means and for variances in view, you can ask what kind of interval claim a sampling distribution can support.
steps.imageAlt: Chi-square densities for 1, 3, and 5 degrees of freedom. The 1-df curve spikes at zero and runs off the top of the axes. The 3-df curve peaks near 1. The 5-df curve peaks near 3 and sits lower and further right.

steps.title: Target Analogy of Confidence Intervals
steps.note: A confidence interval is a range computed from a sample. In the target analogy the unknown value stays fixed and each interval is a shot, so the stated percentage describes the procedure over many samples — not the chance that this one interval covers that value. That closes the path from a curve for observations to a claim stated as coverage.
steps.imageAlt: Twenty horizontal intervals of equal width aimed at a dashed line, the true value. Nineteen solid intervals cross that line. The top interval is dotted, lies entirely to the right, and is labeled miss.

tracks.title: t-test
tracks.summary: This path is for comparing two means when the spread is estimated, so the reference curve has heavier tails. By the end you can say whether the scores come from two groups or the same people.

steps.title: z-Distribution vs t-Distribution
steps.note: When a mean is compared against a known standard deviation, a z curve is the usual reference. In practice that standard deviation is almost always estimated from the same data, and the extra uncertainty shows up as heavier tails than z. Those tails are heavier still in a small sample; that wider curve is the t distribution, and it is the reference you will use for the two comparisons that follow.
steps.imageAlt: The standard normal and a t distribution with 4 degrees of freedom. The left panel shows both full curves. The right panel zooms into the right tail, where the dashed t curve stays above the solid z curve.

steps.title: Independent Samples t-Test
steps.note: One common comparison is two groups that do not share people — each person is in one group only. An independent-samples t-test asks whether the two group means differ by more than you would expect from the spread within the groups, using a t curve whose standard error combines those two spreads. A different design pairs two scores within the same person instead.
steps.imageAlt: Two groups of eight scores. Group 1 is centered at 50 and group 2 at 62, with an arrow marking a mean difference of 12. A bracket of length s = 4.9 sits beside each mean.

steps.title: Paired Sample t-Test
steps.note: In a paired design, the two scores from each person become one difference. That removes person-to-person variation before the mean difference is set against a t curve. The path ends here: the same family of reference curve, and two designs for which scores enter the comparison.
steps.imageAlt: Left: eight before-and-after pairs joined by lines. Right: those eight differences, with a dashed line at the mean difference of 5. The two differences equal to 7 are drawn side by side.

tracks.title: Statistical power
tracks.summary: This path is for the chance of detecting a real effect, from the definition to how that chance grows. By the end you can say what power is and what a larger effect or sample does to it.

steps.title: Statistical Power
steps.note: A significance cutoff is set under the null, but a real effect shifts the sampling distribution of the test statistic. Power is the chance of detecting an effect that is really there: the share of that alternative distribution that lands beyond the null cutoff. Once that definition is clear, the next question is how power changes when the study changes.
steps.imageAlt: A null sampling curve centered at 0 and an alternative curve centered at 2, for σ = 5 and n = 30. A dotted line marks the one-tailed 5% cutoff at 1.50. Gray shading under the alternative, to the right of the cutoff, is the power, about 71%.

steps.title: Power Curve
steps.note: Power is not a fixed number; it moves with the study. A power curve shows how the chance of detecting a real effect changes with the size of the effect and the size of the sample. A larger effect or a larger sample moves the alternative distribution farther past the null cutoff, and more of it counts as a detection.
formulae: power rises with |effect| and with n
steps.imageAlt: Power of a two-sided, equal-group t test against total sample size, for Cohen's d = 0.50 and α = 0.05. Dashed guides mark the operating point where power first reaches 0.80, at total N = 128.

tracks.title: ANOVA
tracks.summary: This path is for comparing means, from separate groups to the same people and a split of variation. By the end you can say where the variation comes from and what the usual reading assumes.

steps.title: From t-Test to ANOVA
steps.note: With two groups, a t-test asks whether the means differ by more than the scatter inside the groups. ANOVA asks the same kind of question when there may be more than two means: is the variation among group means large relative to the variation left inside groups? When each person is measured more than once, that inside scatter depends on how their scores move together.
steps.imageAlt: Two panels with the same within-group scatter. The left panel has group means at 40 and 60. The right panel has group means at 30, 50, and 70. A short horizontal line marks each mean.

steps.title: From Paired t-Test to RM-ANOVA
steps.note: The difference-score standard deviation already has the pre–post correlation built into it. A more positive covariance shrinks s_D: when scores move together, people who score high at one timepoint tend to score high at the other, so individual change scores stay small — and that smaller s_D is what feeds SS_Error. The same positive covariance enlarges SS_Subjects, because subject sums of squares track how far each person's average sits from the grand mean. Together, SS_Subjects and SS_Error make up SS_Within — the within-timepoint scatter that is not caused by time, but by stable individual differences plus residual error. By partitioning out those individual differences, the paired t and repeated-measures ANOVA cut noise that an independent test would leave intact.
formulae: s_D² = s₁² + s₂² − 2 r s₁ s₂

steps.title: Partitioning Sum of Squares
steps.note: To compare several means, it helps to say where the variation in the data comes from. Partitioning the sum of squares splits total variation into a part between groups and a part left inside groups; the F ratio compares those two parts. The same split extends when two factors label the groups at once.
steps.imageAlt: One horizontal bar split into a hatched between-groups part of 2400 and an open within-groups part of 600. The total is 3000 and F = 12.

steps.title: Two-Way ANOVA
steps.note: Sometimes each observation belongs to a combination of two factors, not one. Two-way ANOVA labels variation with both factors at once: each factor has its own main effect, and the interaction is the pattern that appears only in the combination. The usual reading of any of these F tests also depends on a few conditions on the residuals.
formulae: F_A = MS_A / MS_error, and likewise for B and AB
steps.imageAlt: Two panels of 2×2 cell means. On the left the female line runs from 38 to 48 and the male line from 46 to 56, parallel. On the right the lines cross: female runs from 38 to 56 and male from 56 to 38.

steps.title: ANOVA Assumptions
steps.note: The usual reading of an F test wants residuals that are roughly normal, groups with similar spread, and observations that are independent of each other. Those are the conditions for the standard interpretation — a check on whether the splits and F ratios can be read in the ordinary way.
steps.imageAlt: Left: a Q–Q plot of standardized residuals from three groups, close to a straight reference line. Right: those groups as dot plots, with means near 20, 32, and 42 and similar vertical spread.

tracks.title: Association
tracks.summary: This path is for how two variables move together, from shared movement to a share of variance. By the end, sum of squares is the same idea as variance, and positive correlation widens a sum and narrows a difference.

steps.title: Covariance and Correlation
steps.note: When two variables are measured together, a natural question is whether they tend to move in the same direction. Covariance records that shared movement in the units of both variables; dividing by the two standard deviations turns the record into a correlation on a scale from negative one to one. The size of that correlation also has a meaning in units of variance.
steps.imageAlt: Scatter of 36 points with a positive association. Dashed lines mark the mean of x and the mean of y. A label reads r = 0.81, unit-free.

steps.title: Variance Explained
steps.note: A correlation says how strongly two variables line up; squaring it turns that strength into a share of variance. That square is the proportion of variance in one variable that a straight-line relationship with the other accounts for. The last step stays with variance and asks what happens when sources do not share anything.
steps.imageAlt: Left: 36 points with a fitted straight line and dotted residuals. Right: a bar of the variance in y, hatched for the shared 66 percent and open for the remaining 34 percent. The panel title reads R² = 0.66.

steps.title: Additivity of Variance & SS
steps.note: Sum of squares is simply another way to measure deviation — the same idea as variance, kept as a total rather than an average. Because squared deviations are always positive, those totals add cleanly. The catch is mild: since they are squares, adding or subtracting two variables still has to carry their correlation, which widens a sum and narrows a difference when the association is positive.
formulae: Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2 Cov(X, Y)
Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) − 2 Cov(X, Y)
SS(X + Y) = SS(X) + SS(Y) + 2 SP(X, Y)
SS(X − Y) = SS(X) + SS(Y) − 2 SP(X, Y)
steps.imageAlt: Three bars. Var(X) and Var(Y) are each 1. The third bar stacks those two parts into Var(X+Y) = 2. A note says the covariance term is 0.
